```{r m3-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE, comment="#>")
library(postrank)
fmt <- function(x, digits=4) formatC(x, digits=digits, format="f")
```

The posterior representation required for a grading analysis depends on
the functional of interest. Pairwise comparison probabilities determine
additive expected loss, but generally do not determine composite ordering,
simultaneous correctness or the distribution of realized loss. We examine
these information requirements for draws, finite laws, Gaussian laws,
mixtures and supplied numerical probabilities.

The examples use enumeration of small specified laws and numerical
integration of a normal comparison; they require neither a fitted model
nor an optimizer. [Analysis of supplied posterior results](a5-your-posterior-results.html)
gives executable declarations and array constructions. The mathematical
basis is developed in the companion theory text's treatment of joint
laws, pair-coefficient risk and coefficient error.[^theory]

## Directional-error probabilities {#begin-with-one-criterion-and-one-reported-direction}

Let \(\theta_i\) be an entity's target, oriented so that larger values mean
higher reporting priority. All probabilities below condition on the observed
information and the supplied model; we suppress that conditioning to keep
the notation readable. For distinct entities define

\[
e_{ij}=\Pr(\theta_i\leq\theta_j).
\]

This is the expected error cost of placing `i` above `j`. It is neither a
distance between their posterior means nor the probability that a fitted
coefficient is positive. In the tie-free case,
\(e_{ij}+e_{ji}=1\). In general the sum is
\(1+\Pr(\theta_i=\theta_j)\). Continuous marginal distributions alone do not
guarantee tie freedom: if both targets equal the same continuous random
variable, equality has probability one.

The package stores `NA` on the diagonal because self-comparisons are excluded.
It does not store the mathematical probability
\(\Pr(\theta_i\leq\theta_i)=1\) there. Ordinary draw, finite-law, Gaussian,
mixture, and public probability inputs discussed here use the tie-free
domain. Genuine equality mass belongs to the separately declared domain in
[True ties and withheld comparisons](m4-ties-and-withholding.html).

For a fixed report \(g\), grade 1 has highest priority. Write
\(x_{ij}(g)=\mathbf1\{g_i<g_j\}\),
\(M=\binom n2\), and \(N(g)=\sum_{i\ne j}x_{ij}(g)\).
Each disclosed pair contributes once, in its reported direction. Withholding
cost \(\tau\) gives expected loss

\[
R(g)=\frac{\sum_{i\ne j}x_{ij}(g)e_{ij}
            +\tau\{M-N(g)\}}{M}.
\]

The identity follows by taking expectations of the wrong-direction
indicators. Independence between the error events is unnecessary, so the
coefficients determine the distributional information required for this
expectation. This result concerns a particular loss functional and does
not establish statistical sufficiency for the posterior law. The feasible
reports and decision settings are specified separately; see
[Posterior ranking, grades, and loss](m1-ranking-and-loss.html).

## Dependence and pairwise ordering {#marginal-distributions-can-leave-the-direction-unresolved}

The following two joint laws give each listed state probability one third.
They are the dependence counterexample in the theory text's
“Dependence and pairwise comparison probabilities” section.

```{r m3-couplings}
couplings <- list(
  Q1 = cbind(A = c(0, 1, 2), B = c(1, 2, 0)),
  Q2 = cbind(A = c(0, 1, 2), B = c(2, 0, 1))
)
coupling_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(couplings), function(name) {
  z <- couplings[[name]]
  data.frame(law = name,
    states = paste(sprintf("(%s, %s)", z[, "A"], z[, "B"]), collapse = "; "),
    mean_A = mean(z[, "A"]), mean_B = mean(z[, "B"]),
    error_A_above_B = mean(z[, "A"] <= z[, "B"]))
}))
knitr::kable(coupling_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Law", "States (A, B)", "Mean A", "Mean B", "Error: A above B"))
```

Under both laws each entity is uniform on \(\{0,1,2\}\), with the same mean
and variance. There are no within-state ties. Nevertheless, the error of
reporting A above B is `r fmt(coupling_table$error_A_above_B[1], 3)` under Q1
and `r fmt(coupling_table$error_A_above_B[2], 3)` under Q2. The preferred
direction reverses. Independently sampling the two marginals would specify
a third law, including equality states that neither original law contains.

Joint draws must retain the entity values from each common state.
Independent permutations of the entity columns preserve marginal
histograms while potentially changing comparison probabilities. Named
identifiers prevent coordinate misalignment, but the intended dependence
must also be maintained by the procedure generating the draws.

## Finite laws and Monte Carlo approximations {#exact-states-and-monte-carlo-states-have-different-meanings}

For a completely specified finite law, states \(\theta^{(s)}\) and masses
\(p_s\) define the probability itself:

\[
e_{ij}=\sum_s p_s\mathbf1\{\theta_i^{(s)}\leq\theta_j^{(s)}\}.
\]

The coupling table uses that enumeration. In the package's exact finite-law
route, complete integer-valued target states and positive safe-integer mass
numerators share a common denominator. `as_postrank_draws()` validates the
canonical input, and `postrank_pairwise()` retains rational coefficients
using the optional `gmp` package. Its ordinary numeric `e` array is a double
projection. Exact rational coefficients do not certify every downstream
floating-point sum or optimization result.

Monte Carlo input has a different interpretation. Equal-weight retained
draws give the empirical estimate

\[
\widehat e_{ij}=S^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^S
\mathbf1\{\theta_i^{(s)}\leq\theta_j^{(s)}\}.
\]

An empirical distribution of retained draws is an approximation to the
posterior, even though its stored support is finite. Estimated probabilities
of zero or one can arise because relevant events were absent from the
sample. IID and MCMC estimates use the same arithmetic average but require
different numerical uncertainty assessments. Chain membership, original
iteration coordinates, warmup and retained spacing are therefore part of
the input record. Declared jointness or convergence remains an assumption
to be assessed independently.

Ordinary inputs exclude observed within-criterion ties. Jittering changes
the supplied values and can change the represented law; the appropriate
response depends on whether full-precision values can be recovered or an
equality model is required. Similarly, arbitrary importance-weighted draws
are outside the equal-weight input domain.

## Conditional Gaussian integration avoids target simulation

Suppose entities are independent conditional on a fixed shared state \(h\),
and the target for entity \(i\) has conditional normal mean \(m_i(h)\) and
variance \(v_i(h)>0\). Then

\[
e_{ij}(h)=\Phi\!\left(
\frac{m_j(h)-m_i(h)}{\sqrt{v_i(h)+v_j(h)}}\right).
\]

With conditional between-entity covariance \(c_{ij}(h)\), the difference
variance would instead include \(-2c_{ij}(h)\). The Gaussian constructor
does not accept an arbitrary between-entity covariance matrix. Its covariance
array describes criteria within each entity, and the caller explicitly
declares conditional independence across entities.

For the specified fictional law in `pr_tutorial`, the Gaussian formula
can be compared with independent numerical integration. For sites A and B,
the integral \(\int f_A(t)\{1-F_B(t)\}\,dt\) gives the probability of
the same event \(A\leq B\).

```{r m3-gaussian-check}
law <- pr_tutorial$law
gaussian <- postrank_gaussian_coefficients(
  law$means[, "score_A", drop = FALSE],
  law$covariance["score_A", "score_A", , drop = FALSE],
  conditional_independence = "entities_given_shared_h",
  provenance = pr_tutorial$one$provenance
)
mu <- law$means[c("A", "B"), "score_A"]
sd <- sqrt(law$covariance["score_A", "score_A", c("A", "B")])
normal_formula <- pnorm((mu["B"] - mu["A"]) / sqrt(sum(sd^2)))
quadrature <- integrate(function(t)
  dnorm(t, mu["A"], sd["A"]) *
    pnorm(t, mu["B"], sd["B"], lower.tail = FALSE),
  lower = -Inf, upper = Inf, rel.tol = 1e-10)
normal_table <- data.frame(
  calculation = c("Normal difference formula", "Numerical integral", "Package coefficients"),
  error_A_above_B = c(normal_formula, quadrature$value, gaussian$e["A", "B", 1])
)
knitr::kable(normal_table, digits = 8, format.args = list(nsmall = 8),
  row.names = FALSE, col.names = c("Calculation", "Error: A above B"))
```

All three values round to `r fmt(normal_formula, 8)`. The provenance record
is retained because the calculation uses exactly the dataset's score-A law.
Agreement with the formula and the integration routine's error estimate
provide a numerical check for this law. They neither justify a Gaussian
approximation for another posterior nor constitute a validated enclosure
for every coefficient.

### Shared-state mixtures {#a-shared-state-mixture-retains-the-shared-state}

If \(h_s\) has supplied mass \(\pi_s\), then
\(e_{ij}=\sum_s\pi_s e_{ij}(h_s)\).
`postrank_mixture_coefficients()` performs this conditional-probability
average. Each state applies to all entities together. Independently choosing
a hyperstate for each entity would change the model. Integrating over a
shared state can induce dependence even though entities are independent
conditional on that state.

Mixture masses \(\pi_s\) describe the probability law; they are unrelated to
criterion-loss weights. Fixed finite mixtures accept supplied nonnegative
weights summing to one. The hyperparameter-MCMC route uses uniform weights
on retained states and requires their original chain and iteration records.
This procedure does not simulate target draws. Its conditional-risk traces,
when available, integrate out target variation within each state and differ from
realized target-loss traces. A finite mixture of continuous normal laws also
differs from a finite law of target atoms. Averaging moments first and using
one Gaussian generally changes the comparison probabilities.

## Information requirements across criteria {#several-criteria-need-jointness-for-some-questions}

For criterion \(k\), retain \(e_{ij,k}\). With nonnegative decision weights
summing to one, replace \(e_{ij}\) in the risk by
\(\bar e_{ij}=\sum_k w_k e_{ij,k}\). Linearity of expectation needs no
cross-criterion independence assumption. Criterion-wise blocks can therefore
contain different numbers of draws, each preserving its own joint entity
vector, sampling history, and target definition. Row numbers from separate
fits do not create a common cross-criterion state.

The distinction is visible in another complete enumeration. B is fixed at
zero on both criteria. In the first law A's criteria move together; in the
second they move oppositely. Each row below has mass one half.

```{r m3-information-boundary}
criterion_laws <- list(
  Together = rbind(c(2, 2), c(-1, -1)),
  Opposite = rbind(c(2, -1), c(-1, 2))
)
information_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(criterion_laws), function(name) {
  a <- criterion_laws[[name]]
  data.frame(law = name,
    weighted_error = mean(rowMeans(a <= 0)),
    composite_error = mean(rowMeans(a) <= 0),
    both_criteria_correct = mean(rowSums(a > 0) == 2L))
}))
knitr::kable(information_table, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Law", "Weighted error", "Composite error", "Both correct"))
```

For the report A above B, the equally weighted directional error is
`r information_table$weighted_error[1]` under either law. All criterion-wise
comparison probabilities agree. Yet the error for the equally weighted
cardinal composite is `r information_table$composite_error[1]` versus
`r information_table$composite_error[2]`, and the probability of being correct
on both criteria is `r information_table$both_criteria_correct[1]` versus
`r information_table$both_criteria_correct[2]`. Neither law has a target or
composite tie. This example follows the theory text's “Exact comparison of
additive, composite, and joint-event information” section.

Pair coefficients do not determine a total-loss distribution or its variance.
The current package also requires suitable joint target draws for total-loss
traces and its joint-draw fragility/crossfit helpers. Some per-criterion
diagnostics can use the corresponding criterion block, while scalar MCMC
metrics still require adequate retained history. Mathematical availability
and a function's supported input classes are separate questions. See
[Several criteria and competing goals](m2-several-criteria.html) for targets
and [Monte Carlo uncertainty and diagnostics](m6-uncertainty-diagnostics.html)
for the diagnostic requirements.

## Supplied numerical probabilities {#import-numerical-probabilities-with-their-calculation-limits}

`postrank_probabilities()` accepts probabilities calculated outside the
package. For example, the normal coefficients above can be supplied as
directional errors:

```{r m3-direct-probabilities}
probabilities <- postrank_probabilities(
  gaussian$e[, , "score_A"], criterion = "score_A",
  event = "directional_error", zero_ties = TRUE, margin = 0,
  source = list(kind = "analytic_reference",
    description = "Normal difference probabilities for pr_tutorial score A",
    conditioning = law$conditioning),
  targets = c(score_A = "Illustrative standardized score; larger means higher priority")
)
identical(probabilities$e, gaussian$e)
```

This route also admits numerical integration from a specified non-Gaussian
law. It requires matching entity axes, `NA` diagonals, probabilities in
\([0,1]\), and reverse complements within tolerance. Zero equality mass and
zero margin are explicit requirements. A matrix can pass these local checks
without being realizable by a coherent joint posterior. For example,
certainty in A above B, B above C, and C above A is incompatible with scalar
targets, even though each reverse pair could sum to one.

Small complement discrepancies may be corrected only by explicitly requesting
`correction = "symmetric"` and a tolerance. The raw values and maximum
adjustment remain recorded. For a fixed report, if criterion \(k\)'s largest
adjustment is \(d_k\), the risk changes by at most

\[
\frac{N(g)}{M}\sum_k w_k d_k.
\]

The bound follows from the triangle inequality applied to adjustments
over the disclosed pairs. It describes the difference between supplied
and corrected coefficients. Error relative to the intended posterior
requires justified bounds on the differences from that posterior's
probabilities. Symmetrization, grid refinement and a small optimization
gap do not establish such bounds; each addresses a different numerical
operation. Posterior uncertainty remains a property of the underlying law.

| Representation retained | Available information | Information not created |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Joint target draws | Empirical comparisons and joint target states | Proof of convergence or identification |
| Criterion-wise blocks | Within-criterion comparisons and histories | Cross-criterion joint states |
| Gaussian or shared-state mixture | Conditional-law coefficients and source moments | Target-draw sample sizes or general between-entity covariance |
| Supplied probabilities | Weighted expected risk for the supported at-most-G problem | Draw histories, joint events, or an error certificate |

Direct probability inputs can carry optional means and intervals only when
they describe the same oriented targets. Probabilities alone do not recover
those summaries. Native joint problem construction for Gaussian, mixture,
and direct-probability inputs currently supports weighted at-most-G problems.
This restriction is operation specific: `postrank_cuts()` can also optimize
an exact grade count within a fixed score order for Gaussian and mixture
coefficients. Direct-probability cuts remain at-most-G. None of these paths
automatically enables every mode available for draw inputs.

All these calculations are conditional on the information represented by
the posterior producer. In plug-in empirical Bayes, the estimated prior
is held fixed unless further uncertainty is explicitly propagated. A
hierarchical mixture integrates the uncertainty represented by its states.
Validation and accurate numerical integration do not, by themselves,
establish calibration under a different data-generating law. Interpretation
of the resulting grades therefore remains conditional on the specified
posterior.

    chapter 11, [“Probabilities needed for the risk”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/11-multicriteria-loss.html#exactly-which-probabilities-suffice)
    and [“Exact comparison of additive, composite, and joint-event information”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/11-multicriteria-loss.html#an-exact-information-boundary-example);
    and chapter 15, [“Effects of coefficient error on risk and feasibility”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/15-numerical-uncertainty.html#sec-coefficient-error).
    [Appendix D, “Software correspondence,”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/appendices/D-package-correspondence.html#supplied-uncertainty-representations)
    describes a dated 0.9.0 snapshot;
